title: Typed path and query input binding / Response-model serialization and private-field exclusion

blocks.text: A placeholder {order_id} plus order_id: int binds and converts the path value. Ordinary scalar parameters absent from the path, such as limit, bind from the query.
A query default permits omission; without a default, the query input is required. Its type controls supplied-string conversion.
A path value that cannot convert to its declared type produces a validation error, rather than invoking the handler with the unconverted value.

annotations.text: The placeholder binds order_id; convertible strings become int, invalid ones fail validation.
limit is outside the path: scalar query input. Its default permits omission; supplied strings undergo int conversion.
Removing the default makes limit required.
Query string limit=3 supplies the query argument, not the path argument.

steps.title: Test one binding decision at a time

blocks.text: Identify the path placeholder first: it binds the order identifier. The scalar limit outside the path binds from the query. Compare omission with and without a default to determine requiredness.

Then compare convertible and nonconvertible identifiers. Invalid path conversion stops at validation; it does not deliver the original string to the handler. Location, conversion and omission are separate decisions.
For /orders/{order_id}, declare order_id: int to bind and convert the path value. A scalar limit outside that path binds from the query; a default allows omission, while no default makes it required.

Compare a convertible path string with a nonconvertible one. The latter produces a validation error, not a handler invocation with an arbitrary string. A parameter name alone does not make it a path input: the name must appear in the route path.

segments.label: Declare a path placeholder and an integer handler argument
segments.summary: A path parameter is a variable part of a URL. The example adds a post_id placeholder to a route and declares the matching handler argument as an integer. FastAPI uses that declaration to capture and validate the supplied value. The handler searches an in-memory list for a matching post. Browser requests using identifiers 1 and 2 return the corresponding posts. The explanation also states that supplying hello instead of an integer produces a validation error; an invalid request is not demonstrated in this range. The temporary not-found dictionary is explicitly identified as an incorrect way to handle that failure.

blocks.group_title: Bind a typed identifier from the URL path

bridge.before: Watch how the path placeholder matches the typed handler argument. The clip uses posts rather than orders; its temporary not-found dictionary is explicitly not a correct failure-handling pattern.
bridge.after: The clip explains typed path binding and rejection of a noninteger identifier. It does not cover query binding or query defaults; the text teaches both, including conversion and requiredness.

options.text: Omission uses 10; supplying "3" converts the query value to integer 3.
Supplying "3" remains a string because query values are never converted.

blocks.text: Set response_model=PublicOrder on the decorator to validate, serialize and filter ordinary returned values to that model. Define only the public fields so private fields are not returned merely because the internal object has them.

response_model takes priority over a return annotation for FastAPI response processing. Returning a Response directly bypasses automatic conversion and filtering; the application is responsible for its content.

annotations.text: Allowlist contains order_id and status, not the private note.
response_model validates, serializes and filters; it takes priority over a return annotation.
Ordinary dictionary return uses model processing. A directly returned Response bypasses automatic conversion and filtering.

blocks.text: First compare PublicOrder’s field list with the internal order. Leaving private_processing_note out of the public model excludes it from ordinary response-model processing, which validates, serializes and filters.
Then inspect what the handler returns. A directly returned Response bypasses that automatic path. Having a public model alone does not show that a direct Response’s content was filtered.

PublicOrder contains only intended public fields. Configure it with response_model=PublicOrder; ordinary response processing validates, serializes and filters to that model rather than including every internal field.

If a return annotation is also present, response_model takes priority. A directly returned Response instead bypasses automatic model conversion and filtering, leaving its content to the application. Check the return form before assuming the private field was excluded.

options.text: All three fields because they are present internally.
Only private_processing_note because excluded fields override the model.

o1.message: The public model filters the returned value; internal presence alone does not expose the private field.

o2.message: Set response_model=PublicModel on the operation decorator to validate, serialize and filter the returned value to that public model. Define the output model without private fields so those fields are not returned merely because they exist on the internal object.

o3.message: The output model includes its declared public fields, not the omitted private field.

steps.title: Practice: Response-model serialization and private-field exclusion

public.prompt: Define PublicOrder(BaseModel) with only order_id: int and status: str. Configure response_model=PublicOrder on the existing GET decorator, keep the supplied -> dict return annotation, and return internal_order unchanged. The body must contain only order_id and status; private_processing_note must be filtered. Leave the supplied CSV loader unchanged. The declared response model takes priority over the return annotation.

files.content:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
app = FastAPI()
# Supplied registry CSV loader; leave unchanged.
import csv
_fixture = next(csv.DictReader(open("internal_orders.csv")))
internal_order = {"order_id": int(_fixture["order_id"]), "status": _fixture["status"], "private_processing_note": _fixture["private_processing_note"]}

# TODO: PublicOrder with the two public fields only.
@app.get("/orders/{order_id}")  # TODO: configure response_model.
def read_order(order_id: int) -> dict:
    return internal_order
